title: Copper Deficiency in Plants: Signs, Causes and How to Fix It
metaTitle: Copper Deficiency in Plants: Signs and Fixes
metaDescription: Copper deficiency shows on the young leaves first. See the signs crop by crop, what causes it, and the fertilizer sold here that fixes it.
excerpt: Copper deficiency in plants starts on the young leaves and the growing tip. Copper is part of the enzymes that run photosynthesis and respiration. It helps form chlorophyll and lignin, the stiff material in cell walls. It keeps pollen alive, so a crop short of copper sets empty grain. Legumes also need it to form nodules and fix nitrogen. Here are the signs in each crop, what brings it, how to be sure and the fertilizer that fixes it.

blocks.text: Copper is the least mobile of the micronutrients, so the young leaves and growing tips show it first. In grasses such as rice, the newest leaves fail to unroll while the lower part of the plant looks normal.
Copper deficiency symptoms

Young leaves turn pale or bluish green, wilt, curl and twist, and their tips die back. Rice leaves roll into needles, tillering drops, and many grains stay empty because the pollen fails. In fruit trees, twigs die back and many small shoots sprout at the tips, giving a bushy look. Onion leaves turn white at the tips and twist.
Copper deficiency by crop

Each crop shows it its own way. So find yours in the tables below, then open its page for the photo and the full fix, like the one for [copper in rice](/nutrient-deficiencies/rice-nutrient-deficiency#copper).
Rice

Brown gum stains on the fruit peel, fruit that split, and long, soft, S shaped shoots with big dark leaves.

blocks.text: What causes copper deficiency

Peat and other soils very high in organic matter bind copper tightly, so they are the most likely to run short. Sandy soils, highly weathered soils, calcareous soils and fields limed to a high pH also give little copper. Newly drained peat fields often show it in the first years, until the organic matter starts to break down.
How to be sure it is copper

Mild copper shortage has no clear signs, and the wilting, rolled young leaves look like drought even when the soil is moist. Look for bushy dieback in trees and white, twisted tips in onion, and confirm with a tissue test. A leaf tissue test is the best check, because soil tests for copper are less reliable. A DA Regional Soils Laboratory tests copper in soil and plant tissue. In lowland rice, the MOET pots also show if copper is the missing nutrient.
How to fix copper deficiency

Apply copper only after a tissue test confirms the shortage, because too much is hard to undo. Copper sulfate (25 percent copper) mixed with the basal fertilizer is the common choice. One correct dose lasts 5 to 8 years. Let the soil and tissue tests set the rate, and stop once the field has had enough.

A typical spray in a Haifa vegetable guide is copper sulfate at up to 1 gram per liter, with about 0.5 percent hydrated lime. Copper fungicide sprays also add copper, so count them before you add more.

How to keep copper deficiency away

Test peat and very organic soils before the first crop, and add copper only where the test shows a need. Keep track of every copper fungicide and fertilizer applied, so the field never builds up too much.

blocks.title: Too much is a problem too
blocks.text: Years of Bordeaux mixture and other copper fungicides can build copper to toxic levels that last for many years. Toxic copper weakens germination and shoot growth and blocks iron, and heavy hog manure can add to it.

blocks.text: Copper deficiency questions

items.q: What does copper deficiency look like?
items.a: Young leaves turn pale or bluish green, wilt, curl and die back at the tips. In rice the new leaves roll like needles and many grains stay empty.

items.q: What is the best fertilizer for copper deficiency?
items.a: Copper sulfate is the common source, mixed into the soil with the basal fertilizer or used as a weak spray. Apply it only after a tissue test confirms the need.

items.q: Do copper fungicides feed my plants copper?
items.a: Yes, copper fungicides add copper to the leaves and the soil. Repeated sprays over many years can build up to toxic levels, so keep a record of what you apply.

items.q: Which soils are short of copper?
items.a: Peat and other very organic soils are the most likely, followed by sandy, highly weathered and calcareous soils. Newly drained peat fields often show it in the first few years.
